Global re/insurer Generali is the latest to enter the Lloyd’s market with what seems a sidecar-like syndicate as a way to enhance and make its reinsurance arrangements more efficient, while the announcements points to the potential for alternative and capital markets to be involved.

Generali said today it is entering Lloyd’s with the launch of Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge, for which it has now received in-principle approval to begin underwriting operations on the Lloyd’s platform in 2027.

The insurer said this move is “a significant step forward in the Group’s reinsurance strategy, enhancing access to diversified sources of risk capital while reinforcing long-term partnerships across the global reinsurance market.”

Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge will assume a share of Generali’s outward reinsurance placements, across multiple lines of business.

As such this seems the latest example of a sidecar-style syndicate at Lloyd’s for a major re/insurance group.

In addition, Generali said that its entry to Lloyd’s brings “a distinctive diversification opportunity” given the insurer’s geographical footprint and type of ceded businesses.

Generali’s outward reinsurance portfolio offers significant exposure to continental European risks, the company explained, which it sees as a complement to Lloyd’s more traditional global focus. It also provides a balanced mix of retail and middle market business access across multiple classes and territories.

Franco Urlini, Group P&C & Reinsurance Officer of Generali, explained, “The launch of Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge marks an important milestone in the evolution of our reinsurance strategy under the “Lifetime Partner 27: Driving Excellence” plan, with the goal to optimise capital at Group level. By leveraging the Lloyd’s global platform, we can develop tailored and innovative risk transfer solutions while accessing new sources of capital to support the growth ambitions of our P&C portfolio. It is an extension of our strategy aimed at maintaining broad and diversified access to reinsurance and alternative capital markets while adding a further tool to the Group’s risk transfer capabilities.”

Note Urlini’s mention of accessing “new sources of capital” while also citing Generali’s strategy to diversify sources using alternative capital markets.

Dawn Miller, Chief Commercial Officer of Lloyd’s and CEO of Lloyd’s Americas, added, “Our ambition is to attract the leading global underwriters to Lloyd’s, so we are delighted to be welcoming Generali with the launch of Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge. This vehicle will open up deeper connections between insurance, reinsurance and capital markets, underscoring Lloyd’s role as the leading global marketplace for innovative risk transfer solutions.”

Note there, that Miller mentioned that Generali’s syndicate will deepen connections to capital markets as well.

The commentary suggests that there may be a plan to bring in capital market backers to the syndicate, as a result it’s also possible that Lloyd’s insurance-linked securities (ILS) structure might be used, the London Bridge 2 PCC vehicle.

It’s important to add that at this stage, no clarity has been given as to the backers of Generali’s syndicate, whether there is outside capital in from the start, or the insurer is funding it, or how capital will be channelled.

But, given the strategy of ceding a portion of its outwards reinsurance placement to the syndicate, it perhaps suggests there might be more direct participation from other capital providers. As we said though, that is not immediately made clear from the announcement.

The use of the Lloyd’s platform to set up sidecar style reinsurance syndicates, to optimise and enhance reinsurance programmes and capital usage, is a growing trend, often involving the London Bridge platform.

In the last year we’ve seen Blackstone partner with The Fidelis Partnership on Syndicate 2126, while the same asset manager partnered with AIG on Syndicate 2479, which was that insurer’s second such vehicle after the also Blackstone-partnered Syndicate 2478.

Apollo has been selected as the managing agent for this new syndicate.

Reinsurance brokerage Howden Re, acted as Generali’s exclusive adviser on the transaction, working across Howden Re International, Howden Re Capital Solutions and Howden Capital Markets & Advisory.

Massimo Reina, CEO, Howden Re International, said, “This transaction demonstrates the value of combining deep insurance sector expertise with a strong understanding of Lloyd’s capital. Working as one team across Howden, we have supported Generali in creating a tailored platform designed to broaden its strategic options and attract third-party support from across the Lloyd’s capital ecosystem. Interest in the opportunity reflects the continued appeal of the Lloyd’s market to a diverse range of capital providers.”

Vijay Mavani, Managing Director, Howden Capital Solutions, added, “This transaction demonstrates the value of the integrated Howden platform, combining deep reinsurance expertise, capital solutions capabilities and a strong understanding of Lloyd’s capital. Working closely with Philipp Kusche and colleagues across Howden Capital Markets & Advisory, we have operated as one team to support Generali in creating a tailored platform designed to broaden its strategic options and facilitate access to capital from across the Lloyd’s ecosystem. The level of interest in the opportunity highlights the continued attractiveness of the Lloyd’s market to a diverse range of capital providers.”

Also read from earlier today: Lloyd’s issues guidance and expectations for broker-originated reinsurance structures.

item.content:encoded:
This content is copyright to www.artemis.bm and should not appear anywhere else, or an infringement has occurred.

As industry focus grows on designing efficient structures to enable capital to connect with reinsurance risk, Lloyd’s has issued guidance on its expectations for any broker-originated reinsurance structures, which is a strategy that Lloyd’s itself believes is likely to see increasing demand.

The issue of this guidance note from Lloyd’s comes on the heels of the high-profile news around Aon’s partnership with Blackstone on the vehicle widely said to be codenamed Cortina.

That strategy sees Aon looking to bring Blackstone into Lloyd’s, to support a share of the business it brokers in the market, which represents another signal of capital market and asset manager appetite to gain access to broadly diversified insurance and reinsurance market returns.

Lloyd’s framework for broker-originated reinsurance structures provides market guidance as to the approach, its expectations and what the approval requirements will be for broker-originated reinsurance structures.

The Aon – Blackstone news raised many questions, so this appears to be at least in part a response to that, to place some clarity around what Lloyd’s will tolerate and expect from those seeking to replicate, or design different structures to achieve similar outcomes (the outcomes being new capital entrants backing meaningful portfolios of risk underwritten there).

Third-party capital’s appetite to access returns from the reinsurance market in general and business from Lloyd’s has risen fast in the last couple of years.

At the same time, new structures and strategies are making it possible to bring capital market participants more deeply into the Lloyd’s market, in support of syndicates, so-called ReShares and broker facilities. In addition, the London Bridge structures have also provided more efficient mechanisms for routing third-party capital into the market’s underwriting workflow.

Lloyd’s explained in a market bulletin issued by Rachel Turk, Chief of Performance and Strategy, “The growth of broker facilities and third-party capital solutions has created an emerging opportunity for broker-led reinsurance portfolios supported by external capital. We expect demand for these structures to increase.

“We have today issued a clear framework for how these structures are overseen at Lloyd’s that will take effect from 1st January 2027. The framework is transparent, principles-based, and provides the market with clarity on Lloyd’s appetite, expectations and guardrails for such structures.

“The new framework seeks to support innovation and growth while maintaining underwriting discipline and protecting the Central Fund. It is anchored around Lloyd’s cross-cycle 95% net combined operating ratio target and establishes clear requirements relating to market concentration, ownership and capital, governance, managing agent capabilities,
underwriting guardrails, portfolio oversight and eligibility criteria.

“Consistent with Lloyd’s broader approach, broker-originated reinsurance structures are subject to the standard new entrant approval process and ongoing oversight arrangements.”

Facilities have existed at Lloyd’s for many years, including broker run facility structures.

But, in the past these have tended to have multiple markets backing them, largely traditional insurance and reinsurance players. Where as now, we see asset managers and capital markets players having facilities-of-one, of sorts, as they seek to derive exposure to an index, or index of a sub-set of the Lloyd’s markets underwriting business and returns.

As a strategy, it makes perfect sense, in delivering large-scale access to a broad and diversified swathe of risk. But for Lloyd’s, there is the rest of the market and its participants to consider, hence the issuance of guidelines to help the market understand what will be allowed and tolerated.

Lloyd’s has explained some of the features of its framework for broker-originated reinsurance structures in the market.

Any such venture will need to show its alignment with Lloyd’s cross-cycle 95% net combined operating ratio target, while they will initially be curtailed to a market-wide risk appetite of up to 10% of an individual broker’s treaty portfolio that can be placed into these structures.

In addition, Lloyd’s said that brokers cannot own or capitalise these reinsurance structures themselves. Of course, that would be a step too far over the boundary between broker and underwriter.

There has to be a minimum capital participation requirement from the member aligned to the managing agent of 19.99%, while at least 25% of capacity must be provided by the lead reinsurers, with the panel agreed by the managing agent.

Some business is considered out of scope for broker-originated reinsurance structures in Lloyd’s, including hybrid fronting carriers, MGUs and legacy providers, captive involvement needs a prior submit arrangement and there can be no exposure to Cyber war “type 4” language.

Interestingly, Lloyd’s also seems to want to see a commitment from those participating as cedents, saying, “Once the participation cede has been determined as part of the overall proposition, cedents must cede either all of their eligible portfolio with the respective broker to the structure, or none of it.”

While the managing agent must be sophisticated enough, in terms of reinsurance analysis and pricing, to challenge the assumptions provided by the broker.

Reporting and oversight will be key, with regular engagement with Lloyd’s and data sharing, as well as agreed guardrails needing to be in place that the capital provider and managing agent must contractually agree on.

Importantly, Lloyd’s does not want these structures running unfettered, saying, “If indexation of at least 70% has not been reached by year 3 of the structure, Lloyd’s and the managing agent will agree next steps which can include winding up the structure.”

Annual plans and any mid-year changes will need to be approved, as they are for other more traditional Lloyd’s underwriting structures. While standard new entrant capital allocation rules and timings will apply.

Finally and perhaps the most important guideline, efficiencies generated by the broker-originated reinsurance strategy must find their way back to the protection buyers.

Lloyd’s will expect the cedent to share in the efficiencies generated by the structure (both operational and capital) through the mechanism of a client dividend, the market explained.

Lloyd’s stated, “The framework applies to all broker-originated reinsurance structures seeking approval to operate within Lloyd’s and should be considered alongside the standard new entrant approval process.”

Alternative, third-party and capital markets investors are extremely interested in efficient ways to gain access to insurance and reinsurance risks at this time and over recent years Lloyd’s has itself shown that it is increasingly open to seeing new capital enter the market in more efficient ways.

It’s important to have some guidelines around it, so it’s good to see the market responding and issuing this bulletin.

However, it does raise one question. How many similar strategies of meaningful scale, backed by large capital market players (the Blackstone types), could and should Lloyd’s allow, without risking upsetting the broader market’s sentiment and equilibrium?

Of course, if efficient capital can be put to work to bring much more underwriting business into Lloyd’s that is a good thing, as long as discipline and prudence are observed.

But we all know what too much capital can do and there is a perhaps-challenging balancing-act to be followed, to keep the established market participants on-side as Lloyd’s itself evolves and broker’s increasingly marshal capital more directly to risk.

item.content:encoded:
This content is copyright to www.artemis.bm and should not appear anywhere else, or an infringement has occurred.

Moody’s RMS Event Response has now provided an initial estimate of insurance industry losses from recent hurricane Isaias, placing them in a range between $2.5 billion and $4.5 billion.

Moody’s said that its best estimate is $3.5 billion, as you might expect the mid-point of the range and that the estimate represents insured losses from wind, storm surge, and precipitation-induced flooding damages.

Wind damage is the majority of the losses from hurricane Isaias, Moody’s explained, while storm surge, precipitation-induced inland flooding, and the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) losses are expected to be only around $250 million of the total.

Moody’s estimate includes insured property damage and business interruption for residential, commercial, industrial, automobile, as well as watercraft lines of business, and it also accounts for sources of post-event loss amplification (PLA).

We can compare Moody’s estimate to others, such as the most recent from Karen Clark & Company (KCC) that estimated the private insurance market loss from wind and storm surge associated with recent hurricane Isaias would be $3 billion.

Verisk gave its initial industry insured loss estimate for Isaias recently, saying that onshore property losses from the storm could reach $2 billion.

In addition, Euler ILS Partners, the specialist Swiss insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager, put an initial insurance industry loss estimate for recent hurricane Isaias in the range of $2 billion to $4 billion.

Cotality (formerly CoreLogic), estimated that insured losses from wind and storm surge from hurricane Isaias will be in the $2 billion to $3 billion range, while Gallagher Re said industry losses will fall in the lower end of the low to mid-single-digit billions of dollars range and AM Best said insured loss estimates are expected to be in the low single digit range in billions of dollars.

Moody’s estimate is one of the higher, but still all the estimates top-out at $4.5 billion in range terms, at which level hurricane Isaias is not expected to be a significant reinsurance event, aside from perhaps a few very low layers and any quota share reinsurance participations that are exposed.

Jeff Waters, Director – North Atlantic Hurricane Models, Moody’s, commented: “Hurricane Isaias was yet another example of a storm that intensified quickly over the anomalously warm ocean waters in the Gulf, a region that usually sees higher hurricane activity during El Niño years. Thankfully, the storm encountered strong wind shear as it approached landfall, which disrupted its structure and weakened the wind field considerably. As a result, we expect the overall extent and severity of insured losses from this event to be manageable for the market.”

Raj Vojjala, Managing Director – Modeling and Analytics, Moody’s, said, “Many exposures impacted by Hurricane Isaias were also impacted by recent storms like Hurricanes Sally and Zeta in 2020, and Helene in 2024, which led to widespread roof repairs and replacements. We expect these efforts to have improved the risk profile and structural resilience of the region’s building stock to hurricane winds, especially for an event like Isaias. Nevertheless, a high incidence of treefall-driven roof damage in the affected area and potential roof replacements due to Florida’s 25% roof rule, which can require full replacement of certain roofs when repairs exceed a specified threshold, will drive insured losses in this event.”

SafePoint Insurance Company is back in the catastrophe bond, with an initial target to secure $250 million of multi-year named storm reinsurance protection from capital market investors through a Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-2)  cat bond issuance, Artemis has learned.

SafePoint Insurance Company is an expansive insurance platform and in this case the company is demonstrating its growth, by seeking named storm reinsurance across the widest range of US states of any cat bond it has sponsored before.

In 2025 SafePoint sponsored two catastrophe bonds, securing $200 million of annual aggregate and industry-loss trigger based reinsurance from a Nature Coast Re 2025-1 deal in January and then in April adding $150 million of indemnity based reinsurance with a Nature Coast Re 2025-2 issuance.

The insurer has already been to market in 2026 as well, having secured $250 million of indemnity named storm reinsurance from the Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-1) issuance in February this year.

Now, the company is back to sponsor what will become its sixth cat bond under the Nature Coast Re special purpose insurer, and its tenth cat bond sponsorship in total. Read about all of SafePoint’s cat bonds in our extensive Deal Directory.

Nature Coast Re Ltd. is offering investors two tranches of Series 2026-2 catastrophe bond notes that will be sold to investors to provide the collateral to fully-support underlying reinsurance agreements.

Like other recent cat bonds from the company, the reinsurance agreements will protect SafePoint Insurance Company itself and the two reciprocal exchanges it operates, the Louisiana focused Cajun Underwriters Reciprocal Exchange entity, and the Florida homeowner and business owner focused Manatee Insurance Exchange.

As we said, this new cat bond is designed to cover the widest range of US states of any cat bond in SafePoint’s history, as the insurer continues to expand and grow into new locations and so secure broader reinsurance arrangements to protect its book.

Both tranches of the Nature Coast Re 2026-2 cat bond issuance are designed to provide SafePoint and its reciprocal underwriting entities with a source of fully-collateralized reinsurance protection covering losses from named storms across the states of Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and Texas.

Both tranches of notes from this cat bond are structured to provide protection to SafePoint’s underwriting entities on an indemnity and per-occurrence trigger basis, while the reinsurance will run across a four-year period from December 1st, we are told.

A currently $100 million tranche of Series 2026-2 Class AA notes are the less risky later, having an attachment point of $300 million, taking a share of losses up to exhaustion at $600 million, sources said, giving room for the issuance to be upsized from the initial target, should SafePoint elect to.

The $100 million of Series 2026-2 Class AA notes that Nature Coast Re is offering come with an initial attachment probability of 0.86%, an initial base expected loss of 0.73% and are being offered to investors with price guidance in a range for a spread of between 4% and 4.75%, we understand.

A currently $150 million tranche of Series 2026-2 Class A notes are more risky later, still having an attachment point of $300 million, but taking a share of losses up to exhaustion at $1.3 billion, sources said, again giving room for upsizing.

The $150 million of Series 2026-2 Class A notes that Nature Coast Re is offering come with an initial attachment probability of 3.18%, an initial base expected loss of 1.66% and are being offered to investors with price guidance in a range for a spread of between 6.75% to 7.5%, sources said.

We understand the $300 million attachment point in each case is after various inuring reinsurance arrangements and we are told an effective first-event attachment equivalent would be at around $600 million for the A notes and $1.6 billion for the AA’s. It’s important to note though, that as stated reinsurance was eroded the effective attachment could reduce in each case, we suspect.

For a comparison on pricing, the Nature Coast Re 2026-1 cat bond notes issued in February came with an initial expected loss of 1.74% and priced to pay investors a spread of 8%.

As you’d expect, the spreads look lower from the start with this new catastrophe bond from SafePoint, given reinsurance market pricing has continued to soften through this year.

You can read all about this new Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-2)  catastrophe bond from SafePoint as well as details on almost every cat bond issued in the extensive Artemis Deal Directory.

item.content:encoded:
This content is copyright to www.artemis.bm and should not appear anywhere else, or an infringement has occurred.

Josh Wander, one of the co-founders of investment firm 777 Partners, has pled guilty to wire fraud and securities fraud in connection with a $500 million plus scheme to defraud lenders and investors of the company.

As part of that plea, Wander has agreed to forfeit at least $500 million in proceeds from the illegal scheme, United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald announced.

Recall that, 777 Partners and its co-founders, including Wander, faced fraud charges filed against them by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), in a lawsuit that alleged misuse of funds and collateral, including the double-pledging of assets that should have backed a lending facility.

This case became relevant to us, when back in 2024 Leadenhall Capital Partners LLP, the London-headquartered specialist insurance-linked securities (ILS) and reinsurance linked investment manager, filed a lawsuit accusing 777 Partners, its co-founders and related entities of fraud, a case that is still ongoing today.

Leadenhall Capital Partners’ case stated that collateral pledged by 777 Partners for a lending agreement it provided was double-pledged or did not even exist.

Through its Life Insurance Linked Investments Fund, Leadenhall entered into a secured credit facility agreement with a group of limited liability companies owned by 777 Partners and other entities managed by its co-owners Josh Wander and Steven Pasko.

The borrowers (777 Partner entities) were supposed to have pledged collateral that was “free and clear” of any other security interest. But Leadenhall accused the entities of fraudulently misrepresenting that collateral was still supporting the facility and of double-pledging it at the same time.

Now, Wander has pled guilty to exactly this and agreed to forfeit proceeds from the fraud.

“This Office, together with our law enforcement partners, will continue to protect investors and lenders and to ensure that those who threaten our financial markets are held accountable,” explained U.S Attorney Jamie McDonald. “As he has now admitted, Josh Wander used his company, 777 Partners, to steal hundreds of millions of dollars from private creditors and investors. Wander double-pledged assets, pledged fictitious assets, lied about the financial condition of his company, and even falsified bank statements, all to gain access to his victims’ funds.  He then put those funds to uses that his lenders never permitted, including footing the bill for 777’s collection of professional soccer teams.  Whether perpetrated in the private or public markets, such brazen conduct undermines the integrity of our financial system and will not be tolerated.”

The United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York stated yesterday, “WANDER, the co-founder and former CEO of 777 Partners, a private investment firm, orchestrated a multi-year scheme to defraud 777 Partners’ lenders and investors of more than $500,000,000. 777 Partners’ initial and primary business model was to underwrite and finance structured settlements. Over time, WANDER began investing capital in new sectors, including airlines and professional sports teams. 777 Partners lacked the funds to pay for these new acquisitions, and WANDER directed that restricted funds from 777 Partners’ lenders in its structured settlement business be used to cover the firm’s acquisitions and expenses. To steal these funds from lenders, WANDER pledged to his lenders hundreds of millions of dollars of structured settlement assets that 777 Partners had never purchased or had previously pledged to other lenders. To conceal the fraud, WANDER directed employees to digitally alter bank account statements to reflects millions of dollars in cash on hand that the firm did not have.

“In 2021 and 2022, WANDER raised more than $200 million in outside investments in 777 Partners through the sale of preferred equity interests in 777 Partners and an affiliated entity. WANDER misrepresented the financial condition of the firm in soliciting these investments. In addition, in March 2022, WANDER solicited a $20 million loan from a lender. WANDER provided the lender with dozens of doctored bank account statements to conceal that WANDER had misappropriated the funds, spending millions of dollars of options trades.

“By March 2023, WANDER’s scheme began to unravel. One of the firm’s lenders confronted WANDER about allegations of double-pledged assets, and WANDER falsely claimed there had been an error caused by 777 Partners’ antiquated computer system. A few days later, WANDER again falsely assured the lender, among other things, that the double-pledging had been inadvertent. In 2024, WANDER resigned as CEO.”

In pleading guilty to one count of wire fraud and securities fraud, Wander faces in each count a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. He is scheduled to be sentenced by U.S. District Judge Oetken on March 1, 2027.

Luca Albertini, CEO, Leadenhall Capital Partners LLP said in a statement provided to us that, “Today’s guilty plea reinforces the claims Leadenhall brought to light more than two years ago regarding the alleged years-long pattern of fraud by Wander, 777, A-Cap and the other defendants.

“Our primary consideration from the beginning has been maximizing returns for our investors and today’s development will support those efforts as we continue to pursue recovery through the litigation process.”

Leadenhall Capital Partners has been fighting its case for more than two years, a time-consuming endeavour as it continues to strive to protect itself and its investors.

Wander’s guilty plea and the agreed forfeiting of proceeds from the fraud suggests the chance of making a recovery may have strengthened in the ILS manager’s favour.

item.content:encoded:
This content is copyright to www.artemis.bm and should not appear anywhere else, or an infringement has occurred.

US insurer Allstate has reported a smaller $220 million in pre-tax catastrophe losses for the month of September 2026, which has lifted the total across the current annual aggregate risk period for its catastrophe bonds to $3.372 billion.

September saw Allstate’s reported catastrophe losses decline considerably from recent months.

Which has helped to slow down the run-rate for catastrophe losses over the annual aggregate year for Allstate’s catastrophe bonds, which began in April. However, as we’ve highlighted before, not all of these cat losses will qualify to erode the cat bond aggregate retentions.

Allstate started the new annual aggregate risk period that its Sanders Re program catastrophe bonds and aggregate excess of loss reinsurance are subject to, with $870 million of pre-tax catastrophe losses in April 2026.

Allstate then reported a much lower $289 million in May, followed by $563 million in pre-tax losses for June, an additional $682 million for July, then another significant month of loss impacts for August at $748 million in pre-tax catastrophe losses.

Now, the sixth month in the annual aggregate risk period for Allstate’s cat bonds sees the insurer reporting $220 million of pre-tax cat losses, $173 million after tax, for September.

Which takes the pre-tax reported catastrophe loss tally across the risk period to-date to $3.372 billion.

The third-quarter of 2026 has been particularly heavy in catastrophe loss terms for Allstate, with the three-month period generating a combined $1.65 billion in pre-tax losses, or $1.3 billion, after-tax.

Allstate currently has annual aggregate reinsurance protection from one cat bond tranche, the $150 million Class B tranche of notes issued through its Sanders Re III Ltd. (Series 2023-1) catastrophe bond sponsorship.

For the current annual risk period, which began April 1st 2026, those notes attach at $4.78 billion of losses, then cover a share up to exhaustion at $5.28 billion for Allstate, providing their protection across all US states except Florida.

But, those Class B tranche of cat bond notes are subject to a $50 million per-event deductible, which means only cat loss events that result in $50 million or greater of losses will qualify to erode the retention sitting beneath their attachment.

As a result, it’s not possible to estimate where Allstate’s annual aggregated catastrophe losses sit under the catastrophe bond attachment, but the costly third-quarter has certainly increased the erosion of the deductible.

In addition, we reported earlier this year that as part of its 2026 reinsurance renewal, Allstate purchased a new $1 billion aggregate excess of loss reinsurance arrangement, which attaches high up at $8.5 billion of losses.

It’s important to remember that this new $1 billion of aggregate reinsurance limit only features a smaller $1 million event deductible. Given which, it is safe to assume that a significant majority of Allstate’s catastrophe losses for covered events are expected to qualify to erode the retention beneath this reinsurance layer, although a meaningful proportion of the attachment deductible will still remain available at this time.

CCRIF SPC, the regional parametric risk pool for the Caribbean and Central America, is set to make a payout of US $17.4 million to the government of Panama after the recent magnitude 7.7 earthquake triggered its parametric disaster insurance protection under the facility.

This earthquake struck Panama on October 9th and CCRIF explained that based on its SPHERA earthquake model, it estimated peak ground acceleration of up to 0.5 g in the country, the only CCRIF member to experience shaking above the model’s 0.03 g reporting threshold.

The modelled losses exceeded the parametric trigger of the earthquake policy, activating the payout process for the government of Panama.

The earthquake caused damage to homes, schools, hospitals, public buildings, and roads in various provinces across the country, while a preliminary assessment reports 656 affected schools.

The parametric insurance payout will be made within 14 days of the quake, as the CCRIF sticks to its rapid disbursement of funds promise.

CCRIF Chief Executive Officer, Isaac Anthony, commented, “Our thoughts are with the people of Panama, and especially with the families and communities affected by this earthquake. This payout will give the Government immediate liquidity to support its response at the time it is most needed.

“Panama’s decision to secure its CCRIF earthquake coverage through the Fondo de Ahorro de Panamá is a strong example of how parametric insurance can work alongside national savings and stabilization mechanisms as part of a layered approach to financing disaster risk.”

Panama has been a beneficiary of parametric disaster insurance protection through the CCRIF since 2018.

Previously the country has received 3 payouts from CCRIF, for excess rainfall caused by Hurricane Eta in 2020 and an exceptional rain events in 2024, which together amounted to approximately US $29 million. With this earthquake payout, it will bring total parametric payouts to Panama to approximately US $47 million from the facility.

Adding this to its payout tally, CCRIF said it will have made 83 payouts to members since its inception in 2007, totalling over US $500 million, with all of them made within 14 days of the event.

Nascent Re Ltd. a licensed reinsurance transformer owned and operated by Bermuda-based Nascent Group, has issued another $36 million of preferred share insurance-linked securities, across two series named Plymouth and Warwick.

These are the fifth and sixth individual issuances of ILS securities from Nascent Re that we’ve reported on, with all six seen to-date being in preferred shares form, likely representing some kind of collateralized reinsurance or private ILS arrangement.

Nascent Group is a technology-driven insurance management, ILS servicing and reinsurance transformation specialist, with Nascent Re being its transformer vehicle.

The Nascent Re structure enables re/insurers and investors to transact reinsurance on a collateralized basis, through a managed and outsourced risk transformation platform.

While the six issuances of preferred share ILS we’ve seen from Nascent Re indicate growing traction in the market, it’s likely the structure has facilitated many more similar collateralized reinsurance or ILS arrangements in its history that we haven’t seen.

The first issuance of listed insurance-linked securities from Nascent Re emerged earlier this year in March 2026, with a €10 million tranche of OFS Re Series 2026-001 preferred shares issued.

Then in August, we saw Nascent Re issuing $23.5 million of preferred shares through a segregated account named Telford, the second and still the largest single ILS issuance we’ve seen so far from the structure.

Following that, in September, Nascent Re Ltd. issued US $20 million of preferred shares on behalf of a segregated account named Quinton and a further US $20 million of preferred shares on behalf of a segregated account named Stevenage.

Now, we’ve learned that Nascent Re Ltd. has issued US $16 million of preferred shares on behalf of a segregated account named Plymouth and a further US $20 million of preferred shares on behalf of a segregated account named Warwick.

The $16 million tranche of Plymouth preferred shares are scheduled for maturity on June 30th 2027, so perhaps representing a roughly one-year collateralized reinsurance or retrocession arrangement, while the $20 million of Warwick preferred shares are due for maturity on December 15th 2026, so could represent a transaction that runs through the wind season, given the timing.

As ever, we don’t know the actual inception dates of the underlying risk transfer arrangements, only having visibility as the preferred shares get listed.

All $36 million of preferred shares from the Plymouth and Warwick segregated accounts of Nascent Re have been privately placed with qualifying investors and listed on the Bermuda Stock Exchange (BSX) as insurance-linked securities.

Being another issuance of preferred shares, rather than principal-at-risk notes, it again suggests the underlying structure could be a quota share reinsurance or retrocessional arrangement, rather than excess-of-loss. However we cannot be certain.

With now six issuances of preferred share ILS securities seen, they total around US $110 million from the group of transactions.

Nascent Re Ltd., a Class 3 licensed Bermuda insurer, facilitates the matching of reinsurance and retrocessional risk and capital between sponsors and investors or ILS fund managers, providing a way for traditional insurance or reinsurance clients to efficiently transact with the capital markets.

Nascent Re can transform re/insurance related risks into securities for investors and ILS funds, so providing a conduit to the capital markets for Nascent clients.

Stand, a licensed insurance producer with a focus on insuring property in catastrophe-exposed regions, has announced the hiring of former Nephila Capital executive Tony Landi as its Chief Financial Officer, with a remit to ensure the right reinsurance capital is there to support the company as it grows.

Stand has grown from $1 billion of property insured a year ago to now $10 billion and today announced the completion of a Series C fund raise that secured the company $70 million  at a $1 billion valuation.

Backers in the round included leader Saga Ventures, with participation from Lowercarbon, Eclipse, Equal Ventures, Inspired Capital, Neotribe, and Jackson Square Ventures, among others.

Stand has a mission to “to insure all the world’s resilient property, by making homes safer and thus insurance cheaper,” and part of that will inevitably be ensuring it has the most efficient reinsurance capital in place.

Stand uses its Stand World Model to create a digital representation of every home it aims to insurer, simulating how it will perform under catastrophe conditions, from fire, wind, and other disasters. The model accounts for home construction, surroundings, and the weather or catastrophe conditions it faces.

“Instead of waiting decades for history to reveal what works, Stand pulls the future forward. It shows exactly what makes a specific home vulnerable and the most cost-effective ways to protect it,” Stand said.

The company believes this will mean safer homes, given the resilience angle as it helps homeowners understand how they can improve it, while delivering cheaper insurance over the long-term and making coverage more durable.

“Disasters follow the laws of physics, and insurance should too,” explained Dan Preston, co-founder and CEO of Stand. “If your home is resilient, you should be rewarded with a low premium and never have to worry about losing your coverage. We want to insure every resilient property in the world, and help make every property safe.”

Stand already counts specialist insurance-linked securities investment manager Nephila Capital as one of its reinsurers and has now hired a former Nephila employee.

Tony Landi has joined the company as Chief Financial Officer, most recently having been Head of Strategic Growth at Nephila.

Landi had joined Nephila as Head of Strategic Growth for the firm’s Nephila Advisors investor relations and US business development division in early 2026.

Prior to that, Landi was Head of Reinsurance & Capital Management at Openly and Head of Portfolio Management at Everest Re.

At Stand, Landi will be tasked with leading finance, reinsurance, capital markets, and growth strategy as the company expands.

“What drew me to Stand is the depth of the team, with real experts in physics, underwriting, and product working on the same problem,” explained Landi. “My job is to make sure that as Stand grows, the capital is there to support it, from our investors and our reinsurance partners alike.

“We’ll do that by building diversified, resilient portfolios and matching risk and returns to capital appetite.”

The company has also hired Drew Saad as President of Property & Casualty, who joins after most recently being the Chief Underwriting Officer at PURE Insurance.

“The companies that reshape a market for decades are the ones that identify a fundamentally better way to understand risk, and Stand has done that for the homes exposed to natural disasters,” Saad commented. “With the science already in place, the opportunity now is to build an insurance operation that matches it and scales it to every market that needs it. That is the work I have spent my career preparing for, and it is why I joined Stand.”

Stand is another example of a tech-forward underwriter of catastrophe exposed properties and as such its access to efficient reinsurance capital will be critical. The hiring of Landi brings onboard expertise in the capital markets and ILS space, which should benefit the company as it establishes more risk capital partnerships over-time.

Marsh clients are exploring greater use of third-party capital solutions, including sidecars for liability portfolios, as abundant reinsurance capacity and relatively benign catastrophe losses keep market conditions competitive ahead of the January 1 renewals, according to John Doyle, the firm’s President and Chief Executive Officer.

Speaking on Marsh’s Q3 2026 earnings call today, Doyle said short-tail reinsurance lines remained soft, driven by “abundant capacity from both traditional reinsurers and alternative capital.”

Doyle commented, “Our clients continue to explore alternative options to complement traditional strategies, including greater use of third-party capital solutions such as sidecar vehicles for their liability portfolios.”

Casualty reinsurance insurance-linked securities structures are a flavour of the day, of course, with numerous carriers now exploring how vehicles such as sidecars can help them to share risks and optimise capital.

In property catastrophe reinsurance, he pointed to relatively benign losses this year and growing capital as factors adding to competition.

“We expect these conditions to persist through the January 1 renewal cycle,” Doyle added.

Marsh Re’s Q3 2026 revenue fell 6% to $374 million, from $398 million a year earlier, on both a GAAP and underlying basis.

Asked how the reinsurance business will fare given current headwinds, Doyle said, “We’re a bit overweight in property catastrophe relative to some others, and we’re a bit overweight in the U.S. as well.

“It was a noisy third quarter, which is seasonally a smaller quarter, with some non-recurring items.

“We’ve also been affected to some extent by the consolidation that’s taken place in the industry during the course of the year.

“But, again, no excuses. We’re well positioned, and we believe we have the best reinsurance team in the market. We feel we’re well positioned.

“The team sees good growth opportunities in facultative reinsurance, M&A advisory, alternative capital and alternative structures.

“We’re facing some market headwinds. We’ve seen them before, but we feel good about how we’re positioned over the medium to long term.”
